title: 4. Week 4 - Hypothesis testing, significance testing
text:
Lectures
Last week, we explored how two measures can vary together. You practised visualising the relationship using scatterplots and estimating Pearson’s r. We also talked about how we respect participants’ choices, collect and protect appropriate data, and interpret and communicate research findings responsibly.
This week, we learn about hypothesis testing and significance testing and apply this to correlation analysis. We will also practise reporting correlation analysis following APA conventions.
We will make a start with the group project.







Important



Please watch the lecture material, complete the essential reading and then the pre-lab activities before attending your lab. As a reminder, the lectures and pre-labs introduce the concepts and give you some initial practice, and the lab gives you the opportunity to apply these skills in-person with our support.








TipQuestions?



Make a note of questions as you work through the material. These might be answered later in the recordings, or in your lab. Otherwise, please bring them to the live online Q&A session on Friday or post them on the Q&A forum on Moodle.



Section A: Hypothesis testing, significance testing
You can watch the lecture for the video using the video playback windows shown next. Section A is broken into six parts that should be watched in sequence:


1. Hypothesis testing and significance testing (~70 minutes in total)
Our lecture on hypothesis testing and significance testing is split into six short parts.
You can download the lecture slides as a .html file you can open in any browser.
The slides end with a references list but don’t worry about reading what’s in the references list, we give you recommended readings in Section 2.






Tip



The slides presented in the next videos can be downloaded as a web page: hypothesis-testing-significance.html.

Lecture slides

When you download the file, double click on it to open it in your usual web browser for viewing.
There are many slides but not all slides are discussed in-depth in the lecture, some are there to help to visually support transitions between points.


Next, you can see the lecture elements. We recommend that you watch them in sequence.
1.1. We are going to learn about hypothesis or significance testing (~5 minutes). This is a challenging topic. We can meet this challenge by enriching our perspectives to take in historical, philosophical, and psychological viewpoints.


    


1.2. What is NHST and where does it come from? (~13 minutes). We are going to learn about hypothesis testing and significance from two different perspectives: (1.) The perspective of an individual researcher, asking what they can learn from the evidence from their study. (2.) The perspective of someone looking at errors that we (in general) could make as we make decisions based on the evidence from multiple repeated studies. We begin with Ronald Fisher’s ideas.

    


1.3. Demonstration: significance testing (~20 minutes). We have outlined the logic of the significance test in words. But it is often easier to understand the logic if we see how the ideas work in practice.

    


1.4. Hypothesis testing (~10 minutes). We switch to a different philosophy and a different view of the psychology of researchers: we look at the ideas of Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson.

    


1.5. Seeing the Neyman-Pearson approach at work (24 minutes). To help us to build understanding, we work through demonstrations based on simulations of Psychology studies of correlation.

    


1.6. Summary (8 minutes). Two ways of thinking clearly about evidence. The impacts on how we write about and think about research as psychologists.

    














TipTake a break!



Before continuing, we recommend you take a 15-minute break away from your computer. Remember to note down any questions to bring to the Q&A, lab or discussion forum whilst you’re watching the lectures.

text:
Pre-lab activities
The lecture material is designed to deliver important ideas and procedures for learning about psychological science and analysis. Pre-lab material is then designed to help consolidate this learning, or enhance, expand and apply it in ways that set the scene for the lab session activity. We want to prepare you to be ready to go in the session itself and make the most of your time there.
These short activities will help you to connect Week 4’s emphasis on estimating correlations with sample data in R to this week’s work on hypothesis testing and significance.






Tip



Information on the pre-lab activities will follow soon.



Pre-lab activity 1: Visualising correlations interactively
Last week, we worked on how you can examine the potential associations between variables:

visualizing potential associations between variables using scatterplots;
estimating the associations as correlations \(r\).

We showed you a couple of web apps you can use to visualize potential associations.






Tip



Make sure you have tried these out.

The purpose of playing with these apps is quite serious: you are training your visualization skills, and tuning your intuitions. The only way to do this is by looking at lots of plots.




Have a look at this visualisation of correlations by Kristoffer Magnusson.

After having read the relevant sections of Howell (2017) Chapter 9 (see under Reading), use this visualisation page to visually replicate the scatterplots in Figures 9.1 and 9.2 - use a sample of 100. After that, visually replicate the scatterplots in Figure 9.3.
Each time you change the correlation, pay attention to the shared variance (the overlap between the two variables, based on R²) and see how this changes with the changing level of relationship between the two variables. The greater the shared variance, the stronger the relationship.
Also, try setting the correlation to r = .5 and then moving a single dot to see how one data point, a potential outlier, can change the stated correlation value between two variables.

Try the online app on guessing the correlation.

This allows you to see how accurately you can estimate r (correlation strengths) from a scatterplot. Click on “Track Performance” first so you can keep an overview of your overall bias to underestimate or overestimate the strength of a correlation.

New: Try this Guessing correlation coefficients app because it doesn’t hurt to look at a different kind of app.

Lab activity 2: Hypothesis testing for correlations – getting ready

Background
This week, we are going to work with data that we have generated (through simulations) but which are based on data from a real project looking at how psychologists measure vocabulary knowledge.
Hanke Vermeiren and colleagues (Vermeiren et al., 2023) completed a series of studies to develop a vocabulary test for English-speaking university students. Among the tests they developed were measures of vocabulary knowledge (what you know about word meanings) and of reading experience (print exposure, based on recognition of author names). They share information on the tests through the repository: https://osf.io/ef3s4/overview.






Tip



I talk about this study in the lecture on Hypothesis testing, significance testing because there are good reasons to think we might see correlations between measures of vocabulary knowledge and measures of reading experience.


Reference
Vermeiren, H., Vandendaele, A., & Brysbaert, M. (2023). Validated tests for language research with university students whose native language is English: Tests of vocabulary, general knowledge, author recognition, and reading comprehension. Behavior Research Methods, 55(3), 1036–1068. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-022-01856-x.


Aims of the activity
We are going to:

Download and organise your files
Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio
Read in the data
Build scatterplots with geom_point() and edit your code to change how the plot looks
Calculate and interpret significance tests for correlation when you use correlation().



Download the files
To complete this lab activity you will need four files:

We’ll work with an example script called 4141_wk4_lab.qmd. This is a Quarto document.
We need data files called:


correlation-data-n030.csv
correlation-data-n100.csv
correlation-data-n1000.csv

These files all hold scores on tests of vocabulary knowledge or of reading experience.

Different (simulated) participants’ scores are on different rows of each spreadsheet.
Different kinds of scores are in different columns of each spreadsheet.

Column names are shown at the top of the columns. The names encode information about what the column data are about:

[what test? vocabulary or experience].[is r positive or negative or zero?].[is r large, medium, small in size?].[how big is the participant sample? small (30) medium (100) large (1000)]







NoteClick here for examples of column names





The columns have names that look like this (from correlation-data-n100.csv):

vocab.neg.lar.med – vocabulary.negative.large.medium
exper.neg.lar.med – experience.negative.large.medium
vocab.neg.med.med – vocabulary.negative.medium.medium
exper.neg.med.med – experience.negative.medium.medium
vocab.neg.sma.med – vocabulary.negative.small.medium
exper.neg.sma.med – experience.negative.small.medium
vocab.zer.zer.med – vocabulary.zero.zero.medium

exper.zer.zer.med – experience.zero.zero.medium
vocab.pos.sma.med – vocabulary.positive.large.medium
exper.pos.sma.med – experience.positive.large.medium
vocab.pos.med.med – vocabulary.positive.medium.medium

exper.pos.med.med – experience.positive.medium.medium
vocab.pos.lar.med – vocabulary.positive.small.medium
exper.pos.lar.med – experience.positive.small.medium




You can download the files here: 4141_wk4_lab.zip. Usually they will be saved in your ‘Downloads’ folder.
Next, upload the zip-folder as it is to your Files space on the R-server (bottom right quadrant; no need to extract the files first).
Finally, open the example script by clicking on the file called 4141_wk4_lab.qmd in the Files space on the R-server.






Tip



From now on, you’ll be working in RStudio.





Lab activity 3: Beautifying scatterplots

Information
We begin by working on edits to change or improve the look of your scatterplots.
You will often need to change things like:
The colour of points








Figure 1: Scatterplots showing the relationship between reading experience and vocabulary. Points vary in colour











NoteClick here to see how to change the colour of points





The important change is to add colour: geom_point(colour = ...)

ggplot(data = thirty, aes(x = exper.pos.sma.sma, y = vocab.pos.sma.sma)) +
  geom_point(colour = "limegreen") +
  labs(x = "experience", y = "vocabulary") +
  theme_bw()




The size of points








Figure 2: Scatterplots showing the relationship between reading experience and vocabulary. Points vary in size











NoteClick here to see how to change the size of points





The important change is to add size: geom_point(size = ...)

ggplot(data = thirty, aes(x = exper.pos.sma.sma, y = vocab.pos.sma.sma)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  labs(x = "experience", y = "vocabulary") +
  theme_bw()




The transparency of points








Figure 3: Scatterplots showing the relationship between reading experience and vocabulary. Points vary in transparency











NoteClick here to see how to change the alpha of points





The important change is to add alpha: geom_point(alpha = ...) – alpha is how you define how dark (fractions closer to 1) or transparent points are (values closer to 0)

thirty.large <- ggplot(data = thirty, aes(x = exper.pos.sma.sma, y = vocab.pos.sma.sma)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, alpha = .25) +
  labs(x = "experience", y = "vocabulary") +
  theme_bw()










Tip



You often need to style plots so they are consistent with the look and feel you want for your business, your group or your self.

Here, we will need to work transparency (coding alpha) because varying transparency of points allows us to deal with over-plotting if there are lots of data points; this is when many points are printed on top of each other and things look crowded.





Question 1
Create a scatterplot of the potential association in the correlation-data-n030.csv data between the variables: vocab.pos.sma.sma and exper.pos.sma.sma. Make the points really big.






NoteClick here to see the answer





The important change is to add size: geom_point(size = ...). Add in the size = and enter a number to define size (any integer).

  geom_point(size = 10) +
  labs(x = "experience", y = "vocabulary") +
  theme_bw()













Question 2
Create a scatterplot of the potential association in the correlation-data-n030.csv data between the variables: vocab.pos.lar.sma and exper.pos.lar.sma. Make the points really colourful: whatever colour you like.






NoteClick here to see the answer





The important change is to add colour: geom_point(colour = ...). Add in the colour = and enter a normal English colour name.

ggplot(data = thirty, aes(x = exper.pos.lar.sma, y = vocab.pos.lar.sma)) +
  geom_point(colour = "orange") +
  labs(x = "experience", y = "vocabulary") +
  theme_bw()













Question 3
Create a scatterplot of the potential association in the correlation-data-n030.csv data between the variables: vocab.neg.med.sma and exper.neg.med.sma. Make the points semi-transparent: whatever level of alpha you like.






NoteClick here to see the answer





The important change is to add alpha: geom_point(alpha = ...). Add in the alpha = and enter a decimal fraction to define transparency (a fraction between 0-1).

ggplot(data = thirty, aes(x = exper.neg.med.sma, y = vocab.neg.med.sma)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .7) +
  labs(x = "experience", y = "vocabulary") +
  theme_bw()













Question 4
Create a scatterplot of the potential association in the correlation-data-n030.csv data between the variables: vocab.neg.lar.sma and exper.neg.lar.sma. Change the colour, size and transparency of the points all at the same time.






NoteClick here to see the answer





The important change is to note that you can add all edits at once: geom_point(size = 5, alpha = .7, colour = "darkgreen")

  geom_point(size = 5, alpha = .7, colour = "darkgreen") +
  labs(x = "experience", y = "vocabulary") +
  theme_bw()

Lab activity 4: Testing and interpreting correlations
Now we are going to put the skills you have been learning together so that you can:

visualize an association between two variables;
estimate the correlation \(r\) between the two variables;
test the significance of the correlation.







Tip



What we are doing when we do significance testing is explained in the lectures. Watch the videos and come back if you have not done this already.








NoteClick here to see the answer





In the answers, I assume you have done this to read in the datasets:

thirty <- read_csv("correlation-data-n030.csv")
hundred <- read_csv("correlation-data-n100.csv")
thousand <- read_csv("correlation-data-n1000.csv")

This matters because code examples refer to the datasets by name: thirty, hundred, thousand – and you need to use the right names to get the code to work.




Use the correlation-data-n030.csv data: you will have given the data a name when you read it in using read_csv(), use that name when you do your coding.


Produce a scatterplot of the association between the variables: vocab.pos.med.sma and exper.pos.med.sma.
What is the correlation \(r\) between the variables: vocab.pos.med.sma and exper.pos.med.sma?
What are the statistics: \(r, t, p\)?
Describe the direction of the correlation.
Is the correlation significant? Why?







NoteClick here to see the answer





Produce a scatterplot

ggplot(data = thirty, aes(x = exper.pos.med.sma, y = vocab.pos.med.sma)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, alpha = .7, colour = "darkgrey") +
  labs(x = "experience", y = "vocabulary") +
  theme_bw()








Calculate the correlation

results <- correlation(data = thirty,
            select = c("exper.pos.med.sma", "vocab.pos.med.sma"),
            method = "pearson",
            p_adjust = "none")

results

# Correlation Matrix (pearson-method)

Parameter1        |        Parameter2 |    r |       95% CI | t(28) |       p
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
exper.pos.med.sma | vocab.pos.med.sma | 0.50 | [0.17, 0.73] |  3.03 | 0.005**

p-value adjustment method: none
Observations: 30


Evaluate the results

The correlation is \(r = .50\)
The p-value is \(p = .005\)
High experience scores are associated with high vocabulary scores.
This \(p\) is smaller than \(.05\) (\(p < .05\)) so the correlation is significant.





Use the correlation-data-n030.csv data.


Produce a scatterplot of the association between the variables: vocab.zer.zer.sma and exper.zer.zer.sma.
What is the correlation \(r\) between the variables: vocab.zer.zer.sma and exper.zer.zer.sma?
What are the statistics: \(r, t, p\)?

            select = c("exper.zer.zer.sma", "vocab.zer.zer.sma"),

results

Parameter1        |        Parameter2 |    r |        95% CI | t(28) |     p
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
exper.zer.zer.sma | vocab.zer.zer.sma | 0.19 | [-0.18, 0.52] |  1.03 | 0.311

p-value adjustment method: none
Observations: 30

The correlation is \(r = .19\)
The p-value is \(p = .311\)

This \(p\) is larger than \(.05\) (\(p > .05\)) so the correlation is not significant.

title: 2. Week 2 - Measuring, describing, and visualising psychological concepts
text:
Lectures
Last week, you looked at some of the bigger questions that sit behind psychological science: how theories are linked to observable evidence, why our observations provide estimates rather than direct access to the “truth”, and why the complexity and variability of human behaviour matter.
This week, we move from those ideas to some of the practical tools that allow us to gather and make sense of evidence. We’ll look at how psychological concepts can be represented as data, and how choices about measurement, summary and visualisation shape the evidence we use to evaluate scientific claims.

The lectures are grouped into section A and B (relating to the two strands of learning stated above). Each section is split into short videos so you can work through them at your own pace. It’s a good idea to take notes as you go and to have a 10-minute break between section A and section B.






NoteA note about the recordings



The recordings were originally delivered by Prof John Towse and have been selected and reorganised for this week’s teaching. If you hear references to a different week or to something covered “last week” don’t worry about these references! I’ve reviewed the materials and you will never be expected to know anything that you haven’t yet covered. All questions should be posted on the discussion forum and will be answered by Carly. Please do not contact John about his content.








TipQuestions?



Make a note of questions as you work through the material. These might be answered later in the recordings, or in your lab. Otherwise, please bring them to the live online Q&A session on Friday or post them on the Q&A forum on Moodle.



Section A: Psychological measurement and central tendency
You can watch the lecture for the video using the video playback windows shown next. Section A is broken into three parts that should be watched in sequence:

Types of data
Scales of measurement
Central tendency and notations

Download the slides for sections A and B in one go here. The transcript for all the videos is here.






TipDownloading files



If the file doesn’t download when you click on it, try right-clicking on it instead. You should than see multiple options and you can select ‘Download linked file’.


1. Types of data (~10 minutes)
What types of data can we use to measure psychological concepts that we are interested in? This includes nominal and numerical data.

2. Scales of Measurement (~9 minutes) Four different scales that we commonly use to measure our data. These include nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio.

3. Measures of central tendency and key notations (~10 minutes) Why measurement matters, and how to describe your data using numbers and appropriate measures. This includes the mean, median and mode.







TipTake a break!

Section B: Variability and distributions
Section B is broken into four parts that should be watched in sequence:

Variability in numbers
Variability in words
The standard deviation and distribution curves
The normal distribution curve

1. Variability in numbers (~19 minutes) Why does variability or ‘spread’ in our data matter? How can we measure and express variability using numbers? This includes range, interquartile range, deviance, variance and standard deviation.

2. Variability in words (~5 minutes) A short reflection on what numerical measures of variability can actually tell us about our data.







TipFormulae and calculations



John has just introduced the notion of using calculations to measure variability and the broader concepts behind them. You can download the key formulae for calculating variance and standard deviation and other measures here You may come across slightly different versions of these formulae (computational and conceptual) so it is useful to be aware of them. You do not need to memorise these formulae. The important thing is to understand what each measure tells us about our data and the basic idea behind how it is calculated. In the next recording, John will take you through a worked example of calculating a standard deviation.


3. The standard deviation and distribution curves (~15 minutes) An example of how to calculate standard deviation, and how we can look at variability visually using histogram plots. An overview of the shape of data distributions, with features including symmetry, skew, and bimodality.

4. The normal distribution (~9 minutes) Basic properties of the normal distribution curve and linking central tendency and standard deviation to the normal curve.

Pre-lab activities
The lecture material is designed to deliver important ideas and procedures for learning about psychological science and analysis. Pre-lab material is then designed to help consolidate this learning, or enhance, expand and apply it in ways that set the scene for the lab session activity. We want to prepare you to be ready to go in the session itself and make the most of your time there.

Pre-lab activity 1: From psychological claims to measurements
Last week, you considered psychological claims that we might encounter in everyday life. One example is the claim that “screen time negatively impacts mental health in adolescents”. Before we could investigate this claim, we would need to decide what we actually mean by screen time and how we could turn that concept into something we can observe and measure.
One simple approach might be to ask people: “Approximately how many hours did you spend looking at a screen yesterday?”
Imagine we asked a small group of adolescents and received the following sample of responses:
6 8 5 9 7 4 11 6 7 8 10 5 6 12 7 8 4 9 6 7 14 5 8 6 10 7 3 9
Take a moment to think about what these numbers actually represent.






NotePre-lab question 1




What scale of measurement best describes the number of hours of screen time reported here?



Nominal
Ordinal
Interval
Ratio







TipShow answer





d. Ratio. Time measured in hours has equal intervals, and zero hours represents the absence of the measured quantity. This means that differences and ratios between values are meaningful.





Once we have collected observations like these, how can we describe them in a useful way? One way is to summarise the data to find the mean or average value. You’ll learn how to do that in RStudio during the lab, but for now, have a look at the website app: Describing and Exploring Quantitative Variables: https://istats.shinyapps.io/EDA_quantitative/. The website should open in a new window. You may be offered a free trial of the ‘Art of Stat Mobile App’; you can dismiss that.
Choose the following options:

Under ‘Enter Data’, select ‘Your Own’
Under ‘Name of Variable’, enter a sensible label (such as ‘Screen time’)
Under ‘Enter observations’, add the numbers of the observations
Under ‘Choose Type of Plot’, click the box to select a ‘Histogram’.

Now have a look:

On the right, you’ll see key descriptive statistics such as the mean and the standard deviation (Std. Dev.).
Below it, you can see a histogram. If the histogram looks funny, try adjusting the bin size.







NoteWhat is a histogram?



A histogram is a graph that shows how the values of a continuous (or finely measured) variable are distributed. The values are divided into consecutive, equal-width intervals called bins, and a bar is drawn for each bin with its height showing how many observations fall inside it (or the proportion or density). Because the bins are adjacent, the bars touch, which distinguishes a histogram from a bar chart of separate categories. Histograms make it easy to see the shape of a distribution, including its centre, spread, skew, and any outliers or multiple peaks.


Play around:

What happens if you add more observations? How does it change the mean and the standard deviation? What happens to the histogram?
Try adding 10 observations of lower screen time values.
Try adding an impossibly large observation, like 89. That is, of course, far larger than there are hours in the day, but data entry errors like that do happen. How does it effect the mean and the standard deviation?
You can also click the option to see a boxplot as well as a histogram. Can you work out how key descriptive statistics are represented in a boxplot?







NotePre-lab question 2




The mean reported screen time in this sample was approximately 7.4 hours. Which of the following would NOT be justified from these data?



Participants reported an average of 7.4 hours of screen time.
There was variation in reported screen time between participants.
Adolescents who use screens more have poorer mental health.
Some participants reported more screen time than others.







TipShow answer





c. Here, our measure of screen time is self-reported hours of screen use on one day. We have not measured mental health, so these observations cannot tell us whether greater screen use is associated with poorer mental health. Our measure of “screen time” is also only one possible way of representing a complex behaviour. For example, it does not distinguish between different activities or content, such as studying, gaming, messaging friends or watching videos. This illustrates an important challenge in psychological science: the questions and theories we are interested in are often complex, while the data we collect are particular observations produced by the choices we make about what and how to measure. So, even when we can accurately describe a set of observations, we still need to be careful about what those observations allow us to conclude.











NotePre-lab question 3




If two sets of data have exactly the same mean, what can we conclude about their variability?



They must have the same variability
They must have the same standard deviation
One must have a larger range
We cannot tell from the mean alone







TipShow answer





d.

Background
Last week, we worked with some publicly available data from a research project on mind wandering. Gaining experience with psychological research as a participant plays an important role in becoming a researcher.

Taking part in psychological research is one of the most direct ways to understand how research works. A textbook or lecture can only take you so far. Experiencing a study from the inside shows you things that are hard to appreciate otherwise.
As a participant, you see how researchers turn abstract ideas into something measurable: how instructions are worded, how tasks are designed, how conditions are manipulated and how responses are recorded. Welcome
Welcome to the PSYC4141 material for the academic year 2026-2027!
How do we determine what is a true finding in psychological science? How do we know which theories are well supported by evidence? This module introduces you to rigorous and transparent scientific practices. You will develop systematic ways of thinking about and approaching real-world issues. Using modern techniques, you will learn how to collect, present and analyse data. We will introduce key concepts and practices of research design and data analysis through lectures. Practical laboratory classes will teach you how to design studies, handle data, perform statistical analyses and report your findings. The laboratory classes will be hands-on, giving you direct experience of all stages of a research project, including the use of specialised software. Topics covered will include questionnaire design, collecting and working with observational data, and looking at relationships between variables using correlation and regression analysis.


Working at your own pace and seeking help
We have carefully prepared and refined the lab materials in this course over several years, and we feel that the pace of the materials is just about right for our students. Some students will complete them more quickly, and others more slowly - both of these scenarios are absolutely fine. You should work at the pace that suits you best, making sure you understand the materials before you move forward.
It is fairly inevitable that you will get stuck on the lab materials in this module at some point. This might be in Week 1, Week 2, or later. When you do, it’s important you reach out for help:

Ask your friends on your table. We’ve designed this teaching space to help collaborative work. You are encouraged to work with other students. Make sure you ask others to explain how they’ve solved an exercise. Make sure you help out others where you can. Always make sure you understand the code and the exercise; don’t simply be satisfied that you’ve got the right answer.
Ask a GTA or Lecturer. Our Graduate Teaching Assistants are there to help you. There are no “stupid questions” in statistics, so just ask the GTAs any question about what you’re doing. Likewise, ask the Lecturer.
Ask on the Q&A Forum on Moodle. On the PSYC4141 moodle page you will find a Q&A Forum. This is a great way to ask a question outside of the lab sessions. It might seem scary to ask a question in the forum, but please don’t be afraid to do this. If you have a question, you can bet 30+ other students also have the same question! So by asking the question on the forum, you help out many more people on the module. A friendly GTA or Lecturer will be along to answer the question as soon as possible (we aim for within 48 hours during the working week).
Ask during live online Q & A session. Each week we hold an online “Q&A” session where we will try and resolve any general queries and problems. It’s an ideal time to discuss things that students are struggling with or confused about, and can share ideas and answers. You can ask on the discussion forum above and then we might be able to pick up the issues and discuss them, but also you can ask in the session itself.

Asking good questions - It’s really important that you give us as much information as you can when you ask your questions (in class and especially on the forum). It’s so much harder to help respond to “I can’t do Exercise 5 in Week 7” (because we don’t know why it is that you can’t do it) than for example “In Exercise 5 of Week 7, I’ve managed to read in the data, but the graph looks quite odd. Here is the code I’m using…”

Pre-lab activities
The lecture material is designed to deliver important ideas and procedures for learning about psychological science and analysis. Pre-lab material is then designed to help consolidate this learning, or enhance, expand and apply it in ways that set the scene for the lab session activity. We want to prepare you to be ready to go in the session itself and make the most of your time there.
These short activities will help you connect Week 2’s emphasis on data visualisation to this week’s work with understanding relationships between two numerical variables.

Pre-lab activity 1: Why visualise data? Anscombe’s quartet
Last week, we considered the importance of visualising your data and not to just rely on the summary numbers. These measures of central tendency (e.g., mean, median, mode) are also referred to as ‘descriptive statistics’ or ‘summary statistics’. This is because we use them to summarise and describe our data, but we do not use them to make any inferences about our data.
Anscombe’s quartet (1973) showed that four different sets of bivariate data (where X and Y are both recorded for each participant) with very similar summary statistics (including means, variances and Pearson correlation coefficients) can look very different when plotted. You can read more about this and explore the four plots here.
Look closely at the plots. Which one looks approximately linear? Which shows a curved pattern? Where does a single unusual observation have a particularly strong influence?






NoteTakeaway



A correlation coefficient is useful, but looking at a scatterplot helps us spot features that one number cannot show.




Pre-lab activity 2: Visualising correlations interactively
Have a look at this visualisation of correlations by Kristoffer Magnusson.
After having read the relevant sections of Howell (2017) Chapter 9 (see under Reading), use this visualisation page to visually replicate the scatterplots in Figures 9.1 and 9.2 - use a sample of 100. After that, visually replicate the scatterplots in Figure 9.3.
Each time you change the correlation, pay attention to the shared variance (the overlap between the two variables, based on R²) and see how this changes with the changing level of relationship between the two variables. The greater the shared variance, the stronger the relationship.
Also, try setting the correlation to r = .5 and then moving a single dot to see how one data point, a potential outlier, can change the stated correlation value between two variables.


Pre-lab activity 3: Guess the correlation
Try this online app on guessing the correlation.
This allows you to see how accurately you can estimate r (correlation strengths) from a scatterplot. Click on “Track Performance” first so you can keep an overview of your overall bias to underestimate or overestimate the strength of a correlation.
Is this all just a bit of fun? Well, yes, because stats is actually fun, and no, because it serves a purpose of helping you determine if the correlations you see in your own data are real, and to help you see if correlations in published research match with what you are being told. As you will have seen from the above examples, one data point can lead to a misleading relationship and even what might be considered a medium to strong relationship may actually have only limited relevance in the real world. It is our responsibility as psychological scientists to interpret our findings appropriately and to not overstate our results. We will think more about this in the lab this week.

How do we decide whether two groups differ in a psychological process or behaviour? This module builds on the knowledge and skills acquired in Introduction to Psychological Research (PSYC4141).
